evidence_quotes.quote: The overall aim of this paper is to analyse socio-economic disparities in the supply of drinking water in Sweden by using a case study region. To identify disparities, we assess whether indicators of (environmental) justice (including income, age, education, employment status, gender, and place of birth) correlate with (a) the type of water supply (private well or municipal drinking water supply), (b) the quality of the drinking water, (c) the price of water, and (d) the experienced pipe breaks.

The reason why 10% of the households are not connected to the MDWS is the low population density of some areas and the distance to the distribution system managed by the MDWS. Private wells used for drinking water supply are exclusively located in rural areas.

Using data obtained directly from municipalities, we mapped the exact boundaries of areas connected to the municipal drinking water supply (MDWS). All remaining built-up areas, not covered by the MDWS polygons, were assumed to rely on self-supplied water via private wells.
We estimate that nearly 880 000 people are supplied with municipal drinking water in the Gothenburg region, and approximately 176 000 people are private well users.
One explanation may be the structure of the Swedish water sector itself, where utilities operate under similar regulatory frameworks and cost-recovery principles

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community drinking water service access across 13 municipalities in the extended Gothenburg region of Western Sweden, comparing municipal drinking water supply (MDWS) coverage versus reliance on private domestic wells, as well as municipal water fees, pipe breaks, and water quality indicators.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails Criterion 2 under BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study does not empirically examine a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor as an exposure: its independent variables are socio-economic and demographic indicators (income, education, age, employment status, sex, and country of birth) correlated with service outcomes (supply type, water quality test compliance, water fees, and pipe breaks), while all 12 municipal waterworks operate under the same municipal ownership and national regulatory regime. Mentions of the Drinking Water Ordinance (LIVSFS 2022:12) exempting small private wells, municipal cost-recovery principles, and potential testing subsidies appear only as descriptive background or policy discussion. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, no rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, tenure/documentation rules, tariff or connection-fee rules tested as barriers to access, enforcement, or regulatory/ownership structure) is analysed; water fees and connection status are treated solely as outcome metrics across socio-economic strata, and non-connection in rural areas is attributed to low population density, distance to networks, and residential lifestyle preferences.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary quantitative geospatial and statistical analysis combining municipality-supplied GIS water service-area boundaries, Geological Survey of Sweden (SGU) well records, Statistics Sweden small-area socio-economic data, and Swedish Water and Wastewater Association (VASS) utility indicators using Pearson chi-square tests, Cramer's V, Spearman rank correlations, Mann-Whitney U tests, and Cohen's d.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports multiple drinking-water access and service outcomes: connection to municipal drinking water supply versus reliance on untreated private wells, single-family and multi-family connection fees, volumetric water/wastewater fees, annual water costs, network and service-line pipe breaks, pressure/quality complaints, and microbial/chemical water quality test results.
criterion_notes.c5: Population, unit of analysis (demographic statistical areas of 700-2,700 inhabitants and municipalities across 13 municipalities, ~1.05 million residents), socio-economic exposure variables, service outcomes, and cross-sectional geospatial/ecological study design are clearly reported; however, the exposure studied is socio-demographic status rather than an eligible legal/governance mechanism.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English.

study_design: Cross-sectional geospatial and ecological correlation/comparative study
population_and_sample: Approximately 1.05 million residents (~880,000 municipally supplied and ~176,000 private well users) across small demographic statistical areas (700-2,700 inhabitants) in 13 municipalities of the extended Gothenburg region, South-West Sweden
exposure: Area-level socio-economic and demographic characteristics (income, education, age, employment status, sex, and country of birth)
outcome: Drinking water supply type (municipal drinking water connection vs. private domestic well reliance) and municipal VASS utility indicators (connection fees, volumetric and annual fees, network and service-line pipe breaks, pressure/quality complaints, and chemical/microbial/odor water quality test outcomes)
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). While the paper empirically examines household drinking water service access, connection vs. private-well self-supply, tariffs, pipe breaks, and water quality across 13 Swedish municipalities, its explanatory variables are purely socio-economic and demographic indicators (income, education, age, employment status, gender, and country of birth). It does not empirically examine any legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance factor—nor any rule-type mechanism governing service access under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification (regulatory exemptions for private wells and Swedish cost-recovery principles are discussed only as unanalysed background context, and tariff levels are treated solely as descriptive service outcomes correlated with neighbourhood income).
